whatItDoes: Converts between American Wire Gauge (AWG), millimeters squared (mm²), diameter in millimeters, and resistance per kilometer for the most common AWG sizes. Includes a quick-reference table for AWG 0000 through AWG 28 with their corresponding diameter, cross-section, and copper resistance.
whyItExists: Every electrician, engineer, and hobbyist has had to convert between AWG and mm² at some point. The conversion isn't linear (each AWG step changes by a fixed ratio, not a fixed amount), so mental math is impractical. This calculator gives the answer instantly, plus the diameter and resistance for the resulting size.
whoShouldUse: Electricians selecting wire size, electrical engineers designing harnesses, DIY solar / RV / boat owners picking battery cable gauge, audio / HiFi enthusiasts matching speaker wire, and electronics hobbyists converting between AWG and mm² when sourcing parts.

bestPractices: Always check both directions when sourcing — a 2.5 mm² wire is close to AWG 13, not 12
For high-current applications, round DOWN (heavier wire) not up
Resistance values are for copper at 20°C; aluminum is ~1.54× higher (use the material toggle in the voltage-drop calculator)
AWG only applies to round solid wire; stranded wire uses circular mils, not AWG
For very small wires (AWG 30+), use stranded equivalents because solid wire is fragile
commonMistakes: Assuming AWG → mm² is linear (each AWG step is a fixed ratio, not a fixed amount)
Confusing diameter and cross-section (a 2 mm diameter is 3.14 mm² cross-section)
Using aluminum resistance values for copper (aluminum is ~1.54× more resistive)
Choosing AWG by physical thickness instead of cross-section (stranded wire diameter ≠ solid wire diameter)
Forgetting that 0000, 000, 00, 0 are negative AWG numbers — 0000 is AWG -4, not AWG 4
faq: Is AWG a diameter or cross-section? — It's a gauge index, not a size. The standard formula is: area = 0.012668 mm² × 92^((36−n)/19.5), which means each AWG step is ~1.26× the area of the previous step.
Why is 0000 smaller than 0? — In AWG, higher numbers are thinner. 0000 (often written 4/0) is the largest at ~107 mm². 0 (1/0) is smaller. Negative AWG numbers: -4 = 0000, -3 = 000, -2 = 00, -1 = 0.
Does the calculator handle stranded wire? — No. AWG is defined for solid round wire. Stranded wire uses circular mils (CM) or the cross-section in mm². The calculator covers the solid-wire case.
What about aluminum? — Aluminum has ~1.54× the resistance of copper at the same cross-section. For voltage drop, use the voltage-drop calculator (which has a material toggle) rather than this one.
Is the resistance value accurate for AC? — The values shown are DC resistance at 20°C. AC resistance is slightly higher due to skin effect, especially for large conductors at high frequency.
